guided_journeys.tagline: A strange result has sealed the lab. Build a study strong enough to open every door.
guided_journeys.guide: Dr. Vale, the night-shift research director
guided_journeys.premise: A glowing plant has appeared behind the Observation Window, but the lab security system refuses to accept anyone’s explanation. Each room will open only when the investigation becomes more trustworthy.
guided_journeys.mission: Carry one evidence packet from the first observation to the final sampling balcony without letting bias, bad controls, or weak statistics corrupt it.
guided_journeys.finale: The final error-bar display settles into place. Dr. Vale stamps the evidence packet APPROVED, the lockdown lights turn green, and the lab doors open. You leave with one continuous investigation in your head, from observation to uncertainty.

scenes.title: Observation Window
scenes.story_open: Dr. Vale pulls back the blind. A plant behind the glass is glowing when it should not be. “Do not explain it yet,” she warns. “First, notice what is actually there.”
scenes.story_close: The plant’s sensor spits out a blank evidence card. Two locked doors light up ahead, demanding a testable prediction before the card can move on.

story_beats.story: Scientist following and revisiting an investigation map. A scientist walks the route, then deliberately doubles back to an earlier station instead of continuing in a rigid line.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Scientific method.
story_beats.science: Scientific inquiry uses observations, questions, hypotheses or predictions, experiments or other methods, data analysis, and evidence-based conclusions. These activities form an iterative process, not a universally fixed step-by-step sequence.
story_beats.hint: scientist following and revisiting an investigation map

story_beats.story: Looping investigation route. The arrows pass observation, question, hypothesis or prediction, experiment, data, and conclusion, but a return arrow physically bends back toward an earlier step.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Scientific method sequence.
story_beats.science: Observation → question → hypothesis → experiment → data → conclusion is a useful classroom scaffold for organizing an investigation, but real scientific inquiry can involve repetition, backtracking, and feedback among stages.
story_beats.hint: Looping investigation route

story_beats.story: HIPPO writing a THESIS on the window sill. A HIPPO drops a thick THESIS onto the sill, then points through the glass from a tentative explanation card to a target labelled TESTABLE PREDICTION.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Hypothesis.
story_beats.science: A scientific hypothesis is a tentative explanation based on observations and assumptions that leads to one or more testable predictions.
story_beats.hint: HIPPO writing a THESIS

story_beats.story: Optional IF–THEN–BECAUSE card. An IF–THEN–BECAUSE card folds open to organize a prediction, then folds itself closed and slides aside so it cannot become a compulsory rule.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled If-then-because format.
story_beats.science: An if–then–because sentence can help students express a testable prediction and reasoning, but scientific hypotheses do not have to use that grammatical format.
story_beats.hint: Optional IF–THEN–BECAUSE card

story_beats.story: SUPPORT / FAIL TO SUPPORT stamps. Evidence sheets receive only SUPPORT or FAIL TO SUPPORT stamps. A huge PROVED stamp tries to drop, but a metal lock stops it before it reaches the paper.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Support or refute.
story_beats.science: Experimental results may support a hypothesis or fail to support it; a successful test does not prove a hypothesis true.
story_beats.hint: SUPPORT / FAIL TO SUPPORT stamps

Scientific inquiry uses observations, questions, hypotheses or predictions, experiments or other methods, data analysis, and evidence-based conclusions. These activities form an iterative process, not a universally fixed step-by-step sequence.

scenes.title: Hypothesis Doors
scenes.story_open: Two steel doors block the corridor. One is stamped NO DIFFERENCE; the other branches into possible effects. Only testable predictions will unlock them.
scenes.story_close: When the hypotheses are framed as testable alternatives, the doors release the evidence card onto a row of waiting Control Benches.

story_beats.story: HIPPO-THESIS at the left NULL/Ø door. The same HIPPO-THESIS presses a large NULL/Ø plate onto the door and holds a meter reading NO TESTED EFFECT / DIFFERENCE.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Null hypothesis.
story_beats.science: When formal null-hypothesis testing is appropriate, the null hypothesis states that there is no effect, association, or difference of the type being tested. Students should use reject or fail to reject language; not every investigation must begin with a formal null hypothesis.
story_beats.hint: HIPPO-THESIS under a large NULL/Ø sign

story_beats.story: HIPPO-THESIS taking the right ALTERNATE door. A second HIPPO-THESIS takes the ALTERNATE door and raises an effect/difference panel that conflicts with the null panel on the left.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Alternative hypothesis.
story_beats.science: An alternative hypothesis specifies an effect, association, or difference that is inconsistent with the null hypothesis; the exact form depends on the research question and design.
story_beats.hint: second HIPPO-THESIS taking the alternate door

scenes.checkpoint_prompt: What exact scientific term matches this definition? When formal null-hypothesis testing is appropriate, the null hypothesis states that there is no effect, association, or difference of the type being tested. Students should use reject or fail to reject language; not every investigation must begin with a formal null hypothesis.

scenes.title: Control Benches
scenes.story_open: Past the doors, identical benches are waiting for groups, treatments, and comparison conditions. One sloppy setup would make the entire investigation useless.
scenes.story_close: Once the comparison groups are separated cleanly, power flows from the benches into the Variable Control Panel.

story_beats.story: A CONTROL bench is the comparison bench. Every experimental result is carried back to this bench and placed beside its comparison result before anyone interprets the treatment.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Control group.
story_beats.science: A control group provides a comparison condition that helps isolate the effect of the independent variable and evaluate alternative explanations.
story_beats.hint: a CONTROL bench is the comparison bench

story_beats.story: An EXPERIMENTAL bench receives the tested treatment. The focal treatment is delivered only to this EXPERIMENTAL bench, and its outcome is slid across the gap toward the control bench for comparison.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Experimental group.
story_beats.science: An experimental group receives the treatment or condition associated with the independent variable whose effect is being evaluated.
story_beats.hint: an EXPERIMENTAL bench receives the tested treatment

story_beats.story: Zero-effect indicator above the negative-control station. The NEGATIVE control indicator is built to stay at zero for the target effect. If it lights up unexpectedly, the setup needs attention.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Negative control.
story_beats.science: A negative control is a comparison condition expected not to produce the target effect; its exact treatment must be appropriate to the experiment.
story_beats.hint: zero-effect indicator above the negative-control station

story_beats.story: Known-effect indicator above the positive-control station. The POSITIVE control receives a condition known or strongly expected to produce the target effect, so the detector must respond when the system is working.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Positive control.
story_beats.science: A positive control receives a treatment known or strongly expected to produce the measured effect and can show that the experimental system is capable of detecting that effect.
story_beats.hint: known-effect indicator above the positive-control station

story_beats.story: Replication rack with crossed-out '3 = always' sign. Repeated observations stack onto the rack. A badge reading 3 = ALWAYS tries to snap onto the rack, but it is crossed out and discarded.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Three trials claim.
story_beats.science: Appropriate replication and repeated observations improve reliability and help estimate variability. There is no universal scientific rule that every experimental group must contain at least three trials.
story_beats.hint: Replication rack with crossed-out '3 = always' sign

story_beats.story: A comparison clipboard stays on the control bench while the clamps stay bolted to background conditions. A line between them is labelled DIFFERENT JOBS.. A comparison clipboard stays on the control bench while the clamps stay bolted to background conditions. A line between them is labelled DIFFERENT JOBS.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Constants versus controls.
story_beats.science: Controlled variables/constants are conditions held consistent across groups. A control group is a comparison condition used to evaluate the effect of the independent variable. They serve different roles and should not be treated as synonyms.
story_beats.hint: A comparison clipboard stays on the control bench while the clamps stay bolted to background conditions. A line between them is labelled DIFFERENT JOBS.

scenes.checkpoint_prompt: What exact scientific term matches this definition? A control group provides a comparison condition that helps isolate the effect of the independent variable and evaluate alternative explanations.

scenes.title: Variable Control Panel
scenes.story_open: A wall of levers lights up. Dr. Vale covers all but one control. “Change one cause cleanly. Measure the response. Keep the rest steady.”
scenes.story_close: The finished protocol prints onto a visor tray. Dr. Vale sends you straight to the Bias Goggles Cabinet before anyone is allowed to observe results.

story_beats.story: The only movable lever on the Variable Control Panel. You deliberately move that one lever. Nothing about the x-axis appears yet; the action itself defines the independent variable.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Independent variable.
story_beats.science: The independent variable is the factor deliberately manipulated or used to define comparison groups. It is conventionally placed on the x-axis when that graphing form is appropriate.
story_beats.hint: the only movable lever on the Variable Control Panel

story_beats.story: A response meter mechanically linked to that lever. The meter changes only as the tested condition changes. It is the measured response, so it depends on what happens at the independent variable.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Dependent variable.
story_beats.science: The dependent variable is the measured response used to evaluate the effect of the independent variable. It is conventionally placed on the y-axis when that graphing form is appropriate.
story_beats.hint: a response meter mechanically linked to that lever

story_beats.story: Fixed clamps holding background conditions steady. Each clamp locks a relevant background condition so it remains comparable across groups while the focal variable changes.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Controlled variables / constants.
story_beats.science: Controlled variables or constants are conditions kept consistent across comparison groups so they do not provide competing explanations for an observed effect; they are not the same thing as a control group.
story_beats.hint: fixed clamps holding background conditions steady

story_beats.story: Single focal lever with other settings clamped. The cover prevents competing settings from being changed while the focal independent variable remains accessible.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Single-variable manipulation principle.
story_beats.science: A well-controlled experiment changes the focal independent variable while keeping other relevant conditions comparable, allowing differences in the dependent variable to be attributed more confidently to the tested manipulation.
story_beats.hint: Single focal lever with other settings clamped

story_beats.story: The independent-variable lever lies along the X-axis and the dependent meter rises on the Y-axis. The monitor maps the independent-variable lever to x and the dependent response meter to y, then flashes CONVENTION, NOT DEFINITION.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Graphing variables.
story_beats.science: The independent variable is conventionally represented on the x-axis and the dependent variable on the y-axis when that graphing convention is appropriate; the graph type must still match the data.
story_beats.hint: the independent-variable lever lies along the X-axis and the dependent meter rises on the Y-axis

scenes.checkpoint_prompt: What exact scientific term matches this definition? The independent variable is the factor deliberately manipulated or used to define comparison groups. It is conventionally placed on the x-axis when that graphing form is appropriate.

scenes.title: Bias Goggles Cabinet
scenes.story_open: A cabinet opens and offers goggles that hide treatment identities. The point is not secrecy for its own sake. It is protection from expectations changing observations.
scenes.story_close: With expectations masked where appropriate, the result sheet slides under a shutter and lands on the Statistics Reporter Desk.

story_beats.story: A crooked/tinted pair of goggles. When you put them on, identical samples are distorted in the same systematic direction rather than merely looking randomly noisy.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Bias.
story_beats.science: Bias is a systematic influence that can distort study design, measurement, analysis, or interpretation.
story_beats.hint: a crooked/tinted pair of goggles

story_beats.story: Participant and observer blindfolds. One blindfold blocks treatment information from a participant; the other blocks it from an observer. A warning label remains visible: REDUCES SOME BIAS, NOT ALL.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Blind and double-blind studies.
story_beats.science: Blinding can reduce some forms of bias by withholding treatment or group information from participants, observers, or both, depending on the design.
story_beats.hint: Participant and observer blindfolds

scenes.checkpoint_prompt: What exact scientific term matches this definition? Bias is a systematic influence that can distort study design, measurement, analysis, or interpretation.

scenes.title: Statistics Reporter Desk
scenes.story_open: Two reporters argue over the evidence packet. One describes what the collected data look like. The other asks what the sample can justify beyond itself.
scenes.story_close: The descriptive reporter rolls the raw data toward the Center-of-Data Roundabout, where three competing summaries are waiting.

story_beats.story: A REPORTER describes only the data on the desk. The reporter sorts, summarizes, and displays only the values already lying on the desk; nothing leaves the observed data.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Descriptive statistics.
story_beats.science: Descriptive statistics summarize, organize, or display the observed values in a data set so its important features can be described.
story_beats.hint: a REPORTER describes only the data on the desk

story_beats.story: A DETECTIVE infers a large population from a small sample bag. The detective lifts a small SAMPLE bag and uses it to reason toward a much larger POPULATION visible beyond the desk, with a haze labelled UNCERTAINTY between them.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Inferential statistics.
story_beats.science: Inferential statistics use data from a sample to draw conclusions or generalize about a broader population, with the sampling process and uncertainty affecting the validity of the inference.
story_beats.hint: a DETECTIVE infers a large population from a small sample bag

scenes.checkpoint_prompt: What exact scientific term matches this definition? Descriptive statistics summarize, organize, or display the observed values in a data set so its important features can be described.

scenes.title: Center-of-Data Roundabout
scenes.story_open: Three routes circle the same pile of data. One balances every value, one finds the middle position, and one counts what appears most often.
scenes.story_close: The three center markers settle, but the floor beneath them starts pulling apart. The data are forcing you to confront variability next.

story_beats.story: A crowd pulled toward a glowing CENTER target. Mean, median, and mode stations all point toward the hub marked CENTER / TYPICAL VALUE.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Central tendency.
story_beats.science: Central tendency describes the center or typical value of a data set. Common measures include the mean, median, and mode.
story_beats.hint: a crowd pulled toward a glowing CENTER target

story_beats.story: A balance scale averaging equal shares. All observed values pour into the balance, then redistribute into equal shares: total divided by number of observations.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Mean.
story_beats.science: Mean = the sum of all observed values divided by the number of observations.
story_beats.hint: a balance scale averaging equal shares

story_beats.story: A highway center divider exactly in the middle of ordered cars. Only after they are ordered does the MEDIAN divider rise at the middle position, separating the lower and upper halves.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Median.
story_beats.science: Median = the middle value that separates the greater and lesser halves of an ordered data set.
story_beats.hint: a highway center divider exactly in the middle of ordered cars

story_beats.story: A fashion runway where one outfit is worn by the biggest crowd. The outfit appearing most often attracts the largest crowd, making frequency visible without any calculation story.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Mode.
story_beats.science: Mode = the value that occurs most frequently in a data set.
story_beats.hint: a fashion runway where one outfit is worn by the biggest crowd

scenes.checkpoint_prompt: What exact scientific term matches this definition? Central tendency describes the center or typical value of a data set. Common measures include the mean, median, and mode.

scenes.title: Variability Floor
scenes.story_open: The floor tiles suddenly spread apart. Dr. Vale points down. “A center without spread can hide what the data are really doing.”
scenes.story_close: The spreading tiles open into a staircase. At the top, the Sampling Balcony shows why sample means carry their own uncertainty.

story_beats.story: Data dots scattered with different spreads. On one tile the dots crowd tightly together; on the other they scatter widely. The difference you feel under your feet is spread, or variability.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Variability.
story_beats.science: Variability describes how spread out the observations in a data set are. Measures of variability include standard deviation and range, among others.
story_beats.hint: data dots scattered with different spreads

story_beats.story: A measuring tape stretched from MIN to MAX. The tape touches only the smallest and largest observations. It measures the distance from maximum to minimum.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Range.
story_beats.science: Range = the greatest observation minus the smallest observation.
story_beats.hint: a measuring tape stretched from MIN to MAX

story_beats.story: Data points DEVIATE from a STANDARD center line. Tightly clustered points carry short rulers; widely scattered points carry longer rulers. The rulers measure spread around the mean.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Standard deviation.
story_beats.science: Standard deviation describes the spread of observations around the mean. A smaller standard deviation means observations are more tightly clustered around the mean; it should not be treated as a universal synonym for 'more reliable data.'
story_beats.hint: data points DEVIATE from a STANDARD center line

scenes.checkpoint_prompt: What exact scientific term matches this definition? Variability describes how spread out the observations in a data set are. Measures of variability include standard deviation and range, among others.

scenes.title: Sampling Balcony
scenes.story_open: You reach the balcony and see many possible samples drawn from the same population. Their means wobble from sample to sample, and uncertainty bars rise beside them.

story_beats.story: A mobile of repeated sample means wobbling around a target. The sample means wobble around a target while an SEM ruler measures their spread. When comparable variability is held and n grows, the wobble narrows.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Standard error of the mean.
story_beats.science: Standard error of the mean (SEM) is calculated as s/√n and describes how much a sample mean would be expected to vary across repeated samples or experiments; smaller SEM indicates greater precision of the estimated mean.
story_beats.hint: a mobile of repeated sample means wobbling around a target

story_beats.story: A plotted mean standing inside a labelled interval gate. A tag is physically attached to the gate stating exactly what the bars represent. A second sign blocks any automatic overlap = significance verdict.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Confidence intervals and error bars.
story_beats.science: Error bars must be interpreted according to what they represent. Campbell uses mean ± 2 SEM as a rough range for where a repeated-sample mean would typically fall. Overlap or non-overlap of SEM bars alone is not a formal statistical-significance test.
story_beats.hint: a plotted mean standing inside a labelled interval gate

scenes.checkpoint_prompt: What exact scientific term matches this definition? Standard error of the mean (SEM) is calculated as s/√n and describes how much a sample mean would be expected to vary across repeated samples or experiments; smaller SEM indicates greater precision of the estimated mean.

guided_journeys.learner_rule: Listen or read. Imagine the scene. Pause only at occasional Quick Recall cards. If recall is weak, ask for the scene or a hint; otherwise keep moving.
guided_journeys.narrative_design: One palace premise + one mission + one recurring guide + causal route + science-bearing actions + restrained distinctiveness. No decorative event may introduce a new scientific claim.

guided_journeys.tagline: The exhibits have come alive, and an unstable atom has knocked out the foyer lights.
guided_journeys.guide: Mina, the museum’s slightly frantic curator
guided_journeys.premise: At midnight, the Chemistry Foyer wakes up. Matter statues move, ions steal coats, and the bond exhibits begin pulling at one another. A power failure has scrambled the museum labels.
guided_journeys.mission: Restore the museum by following matter from atoms and periodic patterns into the bonds and elements that living systems use.
guided_journeys.finale: The Hydrogen-Bond Bridge hums, the macromolecule crates lock into their proper bays, and Mina restores the main lights. The museum is quiet again, but the atomic rules now feel like places you have actually visited.

scenes.title: Matter Statue
scenes.story_open: Mina shines a flashlight on the first exhibit. Everything in the room is made of matter, but the labels for elements and compounds have been knocked loose.
scenes.story_close: A loose exhibit tag skitters across the floor and stops at the Element–Compound Counter, where the museum starts sorting what matter is made from.

story_beats.story: A heavy crate that depresses a scale and blocks a marked patch of floor. The crate settles onto the scale, showing measurable mass, while its body occupies the marked floor space.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Matter.
story_beats.science: Matter is anything that takes up space and has mass.
story_beats.hint: a heavy crate that depresses a scale and blocks a marked patch of floor

story_beats.story: One pure tile that a chemical-reaction beam cannot turn into simpler chemical substances. A reaction beam hits the single tile, but no simpler chemical substance appears from it.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Element.
story_beats.science: An element is a substance that cannot be broken down into other substances by chemical reactions.
story_beats.hint: one pure tile that a chemical-reaction beam cannot turn into simpler chemical substances

story_beats.story: Two different element tiles locked into one fixed-proportion connector. Two different tiles click into a lock that permits only one fixed proportion; loose tiles beside it remain unconnected.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Compound.
story_beats.science: A compound consists of two or more different elements combined in a fixed ratio.
story_beats.hint: two different element tiles locked into one fixed-proportion connector

scenes.checkpoint_prompt: What exact scientific term means anything that has mass and occupies space?

scenes.title: Element–Compound Counter
scenes.story_open: The next counter sorts ordinary biological elements from those needed only in small amounts. The quantities differ, but both categories matter.
scenes.story_close: A tray of element cards drops onto the Isotope Scale, and atoms with the same identity begin weighing differently.

story_beats.story: A wall of 92 drawers with only about one quarter illuminated, while four oversized C, H, O, and N bins dominate a living-matter scale. Only roughly 20–25% of the 92 drawers light as biologically required, then C, H, O, and N pour onto a scale reading about 96%.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Essential elements.
story_beats.science: Of the 92 naturally occurring elements, roughly 20–25% are essential to organisms. Oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, and nitrogen together make up about 96% of living matter; phosphorus, sulfur, calcium, potassium, and other elements account for much of the remainder.
story_beats.hint: a wall of 92 drawers with only about one quarter illuminated, while four oversized C, H, O, and N bins dominate a living-matter scale

story_beats.story: Pinhead-sized required spice jars beside much larger ingredient bins. Only a tiny amount is measured from each small jar, yet a REQUIRED light stays on.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Trace elements.
story_beats.science: Trace elements are required by an organism in very small quantities.
story_beats.hint: pinhead-sized required spice jars beside much larger ingredient bins

scenes.checkpoint_prompt: What exact scientific term describes elements required by an organism in very small quantities?

scenes.title: Isotope Scale
scenes.story_open: A balance begins weighing atoms that share an identity but differ in mass. The display forces you to separate proton-defined identity from mass contributed by the nucleus.
scenes.story_close: The scale flashes an atomic number, then sends the atom upward into the Periodic Elevator to reveal what its position predicts about electrons.

story_beats.story: An atom jersey whose number exactly matches the proton tokens in the nucleus. Proton tokens are counted; the same number immediately appears on the atom’s jersey.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Atomic number.
story_beats.science: Atomic number is the number of protons.
story_beats.hint: an atom jersey whose number exactly matches the proton tokens in the nucleus

story_beats.story: Several isotope marbles contributing unequally to a weighted balance. More abundant isotope marbles place more weight on the balance, shifting the displayed average; a separate single-isotope card shows protons plus neutrons.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Atomic mass.
story_beats.science: Mass number is the number of protons plus neutrons in a particular isotope. The atomic mass reported for an element with multiple naturally occurring isotopes is an abundance-weighted average of the isotopic masses.
story_beats.hint: several isotope marbles contributing unequally to a weighted balance

scenes.checkpoint_prompt: What exact scientific term names the identifying value equal to an atom’s number of protons?

scenes.title: Periodic Elevator
scenes.story_open: The elevator buttons are arranged like a periodic table. Moving across rows and down columns changes electron-shell and valence patterns in predictable ways.
scenes.story_close: The elevator opens directly beneath the Octopus Valence Chandelier, whose empty arms make the outer-shell pattern impossible to ignore.

story_beats.story: A vertical elevator column in which each main-group passenger carries the same number of outer-seat tickets. Passengers on one vertical shaft compare their outer-seat tickets and reveal matching valence-electron counts.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Group / valence-electron relationship.
story_beats.science: For the main-group elements emphasized in introductory biology, elements in the same vertical group generally have the same number of valence electrons and therefore often show similar chemical behavior.
story_beats.hint: a vertical elevator column in which each main-group passenger carries the same number of outer-seat tickets

story_beats.story: A horizontal floor where every atom model displays the same number of occupied shell rings. Atom models move along one horizontal floor while the number of occupied principal shells stays constant.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Period / electron-shell relationship.
story_beats.science: Elements in the same horizontal period have the same number of occupied principal electron shells in the simplified shell model used in introductory biology.
story_beats.hint: a horizontal floor where every atom model displays the same number of occupied shell rings

scenes.checkpoint_prompt: Without mnemonic wording, explain the scientific relationship represented here: For the main-group elements emphasized in introductory biology, elements in the same vertical group generally have the same number of valence electrons and therefore often show similar chemical behavior.

scenes.title: Octopus Valence Chandelier
scenes.story_open: Above you hangs an eight-armed chandelier. Empty outer positions make the entire fixture feel unfinished until the valence pattern is satisfied.
scenes.story_close: One unfinished arm grabs an electron rope and yanks you toward the Electronegativity Magnet Wall.

story_beats.story: Only the atom model’s outermost electron balcony illuminated. Every inner ring goes dark while the outermost electron-bearing ring remains lit.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Valence shell.
story_beats.science: The valence shell is the outermost electron shell of an atom.
story_beats.hint: only the atom model’s outermost electron balcony illuminated

story_beats.story: An octopus arranging eight seats beneath a large exceptions-exist tag. The octopus fills an eight-seat outer ring, then an EXCEPTIONS EXIST shutter prevents the scene from becoming a universal law.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Octet rule.
story_beats.science: Atoms with incomplete valence shells often form bonds that produce more stable valence-shell arrangements. The octet rule is a useful heuristic for many main-group atoms, but it is not a universal rule and atoms do not literally 'want' electrons.
story_beats.hint: OCT- → eight

scenes.checkpoint_prompt: What exact scientific term names the outermost electron shell of an atom?

scenes.title: Electronegativity Magnet Wall
scenes.story_open: A wall magnet starts pulling shared electrons harder toward some atoms than others. Mina grins. “Now the museum can finally explain why bonds do not all share equally.”
scenes.story_close: The unequal pull snaps the rope onto the Covalent Tug-of-War Table, where equal and unequal sharing become visible side by side.

story_beats.story: A connector that holds two particles together even when the connector style changes. One connector shares an electron pair and another joins opposite charges, but both visibly hold particles together.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Chemical bond.
story_beats.science: A chemical bond is an attraction that holds atoms or ions together. Covalent bonds involve shared electron pairs; ionic bonds are electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
story_beats.hint: a connector that holds two particles together even when the connector style changes

story_beats.story: A magnet that pulls a shared negative electron token toward one atom model. The magnet strengthens and the shared electron token shifts more strongly toward that atom.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Electronegativity.
story_beats.science: Electronegativity is the measure of an atom's ability to attract electrons to itself.
story_beats.hint: ELECTRON magnet

story_beats.story: A magnet-strength arrow that grows generally stronger moving right across a row and upward in a column. The magnet icon grows along the rightward/upward route and weakens in the opposite directions.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Electronegativity trend.
story_beats.science: The PPT visual indicates electronegativity generally increases across a period and decreases down a group.
story_beats.hint: a magnet-strength arrow that grows generally stronger moving right across a row and upward in a column

scenes.checkpoint_prompt: What exact scientific term names an attraction that holds atoms or ions together?

scenes.title: Covalent Tug-of-War Table
scenes.story_open: Two atoms grab the same electron rope. Sometimes the pull is even. Sometimes one side wins part of the charge without taking the electrons completely.
scenes.story_close: One contestant finally takes the electron completely. An alarm sends both newly charged atoms racing to the Ion Coat Check.

story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Covalent bond.
story_beats.science: Covalent bonds involve sharing electrons; single, double, and triple bonds share one, two, and three electron pairs respectively.
story_beats.hint: CO-own shared electrons

story_beats.story: Two atoms pulling a shared electron rope equally from opposite sides. The rope stays centered and no partial-charge imbalance appears.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Nonpolar covalent bond.

story_beats.story: One atom pulling the shared electron rope farther toward itself while small partial-charge markers appear. The shared electron rope shifts off center; the stronger-pulling side gains a partial negative region and the other a partial positive region.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Polar covalent bond.
story_beats.science: In a polar covalent bond, electrons are shared unequally, producing partial charges.

scenes.title: Ion Coat Check
scenes.story_open: At the coat check, one atom hands over an electron coat and another accepts it. The resulting opposite charges immediately pull together.
scenes.story_close: The opposite charges lock together, but a weaker attraction begins flickering across the next corridor: the Hydrogen-Bond Bridge.

story_beats.story: Oppositely charged ion models snapping together only after an electron-transfer arrow has disappeared. An electron-transfer arrow creates the charged particles, then vanishes; the opposite charges remain held together by attraction.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Ionic bond.
story_beats.science: An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Electron transfer may create the ions, but the electron transfer itself is not the ionic bond.
story_beats.hint: oppositely charged ion models snapping together only after an electron-transfer arrow has disappeared

story_beats.story: A cat wearing a large plus badge. The plus-marked cat snaps toward the negative ion across the coat-check rail.

scenes.title: Hydrogen-Bond Bridge

scenes.story_close: The bridge leads into the biological wing, where crates of C, H, and O are already being unloaded beside the Macromolecule Element Crates.

story_beats.story: A partially positive H, still covalently attached to its own electronegative atom, reaching by a dashed handshake toward another electronegative atom. story_beats.science: A hydrogen bond is a noncovalent attraction involving a partially positive hydrogen atom covalently bonded to an electronegative atom and another electronegative atom. Hydrogen bonds can occur between molecules or within large biological molecules.

guided_journeys.tagline: The hotel’s water system is behaving impossibly. Reach the rooftop reservoir before the building overheats.
guided_journeys.premise: You step into a luxury hotel built around a giant indoor atrium. A pipe bursts. Water clings to walls, climbs narrow tubes, resists heating, cools rooms as it evaporates, and freezes into floating platforms. None of it behaves like ordinary decoration.
guided_journeys.mission: Follow the escaping water upward through the atrium, understand each strange behavior, and reach the rooftop control gate before the hotel’s thermal system fails.
guided_journeys.finale: At the Buffer Gate, the final chemical alarm steadies. Mara closes the emergency valve. Looking back down through the atrium, every earlier water behavior now belongs to the same molecule and the same web of hydrogen-bond-driven properties.

scenes.title: Polar Waterfall
scenes.story_open: At the waterfall, every water molecule behaves like a tiny uneven charge compass. Oxygen pulls shared electrons more strongly, creating partial charges.
scenes.story_close: Those partial charges make neighboring molecules tug at one another, dragging the flood toward the Cohesion Pool.

story_beats.story: A water molecule acts like a tiny charge compass while oxygen pulls the shared O–H electron ropes more strongly.. The electron cloud shifts toward oxygen, establishing unequal sharing across the O–H bonds.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Water polarity.
story_beats.science: Water is polar because oxygen and hydrogen share electrons unequally in polar covalent O–H bonds.
story_beats.hint: tiny water charge compass with oxygen pulling the electron ropes

story_beats.story: The charge compass plate has one oxygen-facing side and two hydrogen-facing sides.. After the unequal pull, the oxygen side settles at partial negative while both hydrogen sides settle at partial positive.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Partial charges.
story_beats.science: Unequal electron sharing gives oxygen a partial negative charge and hydrogens partial positive charges.
story_beats.hint: The charge compass plate has one oxygen-facing side and two hydrogen-facing sides.

story_beats.story: Two neighboring polar water molecules approach while their covalent O–H bonds remain solid and intact.. A dashed interaction forms between opposite partial-charge regions of neighboring molecules while the solid O–H covalent bonds remain visibly different.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Water polarity enables hydrogen bonding.
story_beats.science: Water polarity contributes to hydrogen bonding between water molecules and within/between biological molecules.
story_beats.hint: Two neighboring polar water molecules approach while their covalent O–H bonds remain solid and intact.

scenes.title: Cohesion Pool
scenes.story_open: The flood reaches the pool. Water molecules cling to one another so strongly that the surface tightens, while other droplets stick to a different polar wall.
scenes.story_close: The surface stretches and droplets cling to the walls. A narrow emergency tube above the pool begins pulling the water upward into Xylem Tower.

story_beats.story: Two matching CO-water droplets pull together and hug at the center of the pool.. Only water-to-water partners join the cluster, making the same-kind attraction unmistakable.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Cohesion.
story_beats.science: Cohesion is attraction among molecules of the same kind; PPT connects water cohesion to hydrogen bonding.
story_beats.hint: CO-water droplets hugging one another

story_beats.story: The top layer of the pool stretches like a taut trampoline while molecules beneath it pull inward.. The surface resists disruption because cohesive interactions create a greater inward pull on surface molecules.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Surface tension.
story_beats.science: Surface tension results from cohesive interactions among water molecules at the surface; PPT describes greater inward pull on surface molecules.
story_beats.hint: taut water-surface trampoline

story_beats.story: A water droplet sticks to a different polar wall using a single oversized adhesive strip.. The droplet remains attached to the other surface while the water-to-water cluster stays separate in the center.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Adhesion.
story_beats.science: Adhesion is attraction of water to other polar or charged substances.
story_beats.hint: water stuck to another surface with giant ADHESIVE tape

scenes.title: Xylem Tower
scenes.story_open: A narrow emergency tube runs up the tower. Water begins climbing it, held together as a column and helped by attraction to the tube walls.
scenes.story_close: The rising column reaches the hotel heating pipes, where the water is forced into the Thermal Bath.

story_beats.story: A continuous chain of water droplets holds together inside the vertical tube.. When the top droplet rises, the connected droplets remain associated as the column moves upward against gravity.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Cohesion and plant transport.
story_beats.science: PPT connects water cohesion to transport of water and nutrients against gravity in plants.
story_beats.hint: A continuous chain of water droplets holds together inside the vertical tube.

story_beats.story: Water droplets touch the inner xylem/cell-wall rail and cling to it.. The attached droplets resist slipping downward while the central water chain remains distinct.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Adhesion in xylem.
story_beats.science: PPT connects adhesion to water clinging to xylem/cell walls and resisting downward pull of gravity.
story_beats.hint: Water droplets touch the inner xylem/cell-wall rail and cling to it.

story_beats.story: A water droplet wearing a small CAP enters the narrow side tube while neighboring droplets remain connected behind it.. The water column rises as water-to-water cohesion and water-to-surface adhesion act together.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Capillary action.
story_beats.science: Cohesion among water molecules and adhesion to hydrophilic surfaces together contribute to capillary movement in narrow spaces and to water transport in plants. Do not encode 'adhesion must be greater than cohesion' as a universal condition.

scenes.title: Thermal Bath
scenes.story_open: The heating system surges. The water bath absorbs packet after packet of energy while its temperature changes only gradually.
scenes.story_close: The bath absorbs so much heat that steam begins escaping toward the Evaporation Balcony.

story_beats.story: A large water reservoir accepts repeated packets of heat while its thermometer moves only gradually.. A neighboring comparison reservoir with lower heat capacity changes temperature more quickly under the same conceptual heat input.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is High specific heat capacity.
story_beats.science: Water resists temperature change; the CED links high specific heat capacity to maintenance of homeostatic body temperature.

story_beats.story: Hydrogen-bond locks repeatedly open and re-form as energy moves through the bath.. Energy is absorbed when the interactions are disrupted and released when the interactions form again.

scenes.story_close: Evaporation cools the balcony, but the escaping water condenses and freezes farther down the service corridor at Ice Lake.

scenes.title: Ice Lake
scenes.story_open: The service corridor opens onto a frozen indoor lake. Strangely, the ice floats. Beneath it, liquid water remains protected.
scenes.story_close: The floating ice exposes a service hatch beneath it. The hatch opens directly behind the Solution Bar.

story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Ice hydrogen-bond lattice.

guided_journeys.tagline: The macromolecule factory is stuck halfway between building and breaking.
guided_journeys.premise: A giant conveyor is carrying monomers into the Polymer Assembly Hall, but the line has jammed. One station keeps welding units together while another keeps washing them apart.
guided_journeys.mission: Get the line moving again by sorting monomers and polymers, controlling dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis, and shipping the four macromolecule classes to the correct bays.
guided_journeys.finale: The last crate rolls onto the Comparison Shipping Board. Pip throws the master switch, and the whole hall finally moves in one direction. Building and breaking now feel like opposite operations on the same assembly line.

scenes.title: Macromolecule Receiving Dock
scenes.story_open: Pip meets you beside four incoming crates. Proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, and lipids are arriving, but the assembly line first needs the difference between a building unit and a larger structure.
scenes.story_close: A loose monomer rolls off a crate and jams the Dehydration Welder, forcing the line to show exactly how smaller units become larger ones.

story_beats.story: Four receiving bays for carbohydrate, protein, nucleic-acid, and lipid cargo. Three bays accept repeating-unit chains, while the lipid bay carries a clear “not a true polymer” marker.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Four macromolecule classes.
story_beats.science: Campbell groups carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids as the four major classes of large biological molecules. Carbohydrates, proteins, and nucleic acids include polymers; lipids do not include true polymers and are grouped largely by their hydrophobic properties.

scenes.title: Hydrolysis Wash Station
scenes.story_open: The next station reverses the job. Water is used as bonds are cleaved and larger structures are broken into smaller pieces.
scenes.story_close: With building and breaking restored, the products finally reach the Comparison Shipping Board for one last class-by-class check.

story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Hydrolysis.
story_beats.science: Hydrolysis cleaves covalent bonds and breaks polymers into smaller molecules by adding water across the bond.

guided_journeys.tagline: Someone has swapped the greenhouse’s energy stores and structural materials.
guided_journeys.premise: The Carbohydrate Greenhouse opens to chaos. Sweet seedlings are in the wrong beds, storage jars are mixed with structural fibers, and a suspicious alpha/beta path keeps redirecting the vines.
guided_journeys.mission: Follow the sugar trail from single units to larger carbohydrates, recover the storage molecules, rebuild the structural walls, and discover how some animals gain access to cellulose with microbial help.
guided_journeys.finale: At the Cellulose Fiber Barn, the missing feed labels are recovered and the symbiotic microbes return to work. Suki closes the greenhouse ledger. One sugar route now connects small building blocks, storage, structure, linkage, and digestion.

scenes.story_close: A sugar seedling grows toward the Sucrose Trellis, where single units begin pairing into larger carbohydrates.

scenes.story_open: The vine keeps growing. Repeated sugar units extend into long polysaccharide structures.
scenes.story_close: The long chains split into two corridors: one leads to the Storage Pantry Alcove and the other will eventually become structural material.

scenes.title: Storage Pantry Alcove
scenes.story_open: Two storage doors open. Plants stock starch here; animals store glycogen in a more highly branched form.
scenes.story_close: A burst storage jar sends sugar chains across the hall and into the Structural Wall Alcove, where similar units serve a completely different role.

scenes.title: Glycosidic Archway
scenes.story_open: A sugar arch locks units together with glycosidic linkages. Nearby, alpha and beta glucose orientations send polymers toward different architectures.
scenes.story_close: The arch forks at an alpha/beta marker, forcing you onto the Alpha/Beta Path to see how a small orientation difference changes the polymer.

story_beats.story: A GLYCO bridge covalently joining two monosaccharide rings. The bridge forms a covalent connection between two monosaccharides; a small 1→4 case-study marker can appear without requiring exact polymer reproduction.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Glycosidic linkage.
story_beats.science: A glycosidic linkage is a covalent bond joining monosaccharides. In the packet's starch/cellulose case study, 1→4 linkages connect carbon 1 of one glucose to carbon 4 of the next.
story_beats.hint: a GLYCO sugar bridge joining two sugar units

story_beats.story: Greek α and β markers beside glucose rings with opposite carbon-1 hydroxyl orientations. The carbon-1 hydroxyl orientation is shown one way in the α model and the opposite way in the β model.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Alpha and beta glucose.
story_beats.science: Alpha and beta glucose differ in the orientation of the hydroxyl group attached to carbon 1 when glucose forms a ring. Campbell uses this distinction to explain different glycosidic linkages in starch and cellulose. scenes.title: Alpha/Beta Path
scenes.story_open: Two paths look almost identical at the first glucose unit, then diverge into storage-friendly starch and straight cellulose fibers.
scenes.story_close: The cellulose path ends at a barn full of plant fiber that the animals cannot digest alone. The final clue is inside the Cellulose Fiber Barn.

story_beats.story: An α track curling/branching toward storage while a β track runs straight into aligned chains. The α-linked route produces a starch-like helical/branch-capable storage form, while the β-linked route produces straight unbranched cellulose chains that align.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Starch versus cellulose structure.
story_beats.science: Starch contains alpha-glucose linkages that produce storage structures that may be helical and, in amylopectin, branched. Cellulose contains beta-glucose linkages; its chains are straight and unbranched and can align into strong hydrogen-bonded microfibrils. The exact polymer structures are teacher-enrichment, not current AP-required structural recall.
story_beats.hint: an α track curling/branching toward storage while a β track runs straight into aligned chains

story_beats.story: Parallel cellulose chains held side by side by dashed hydrogen-bond crosslinks. Hydrogen bonds form between neighboring parallel cellulose chains, grouping them into strong microfibrils.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Cellulose fiber organization.
story_beats.science: Parallel cellulose chains can form hydrogen bonds with one another, grouping the chains into strong microfibrils that contribute mechanical strength to plant cell walls.
story_beats.hint: parallel cellulose chains held side by side by dashed hydrogen-bond crosslinks

scenes.title: Cellulose Fiber Barn
scenes.story_open: At the barn, cellulose-rich feed reaches animals that cannot digest it alone. Symbiotic microbes do the chemical work their hosts cannot.

story_beats.story: Cellulose fibers stopping at an animal-enzyme gate while mutualistic microbes open a fermentation route. The animal’s own enzyme gate cannot hydrolyze cellulose, but mutualistic microorganisms ferment the cellulose in a specialized digestive compartment.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Cellulose digestion by symbiotic microbes.
story_beats.science: Animals do not produce cellulase enzymes that hydrolyze cellulose. Cellulose-digesting herbivores obtain access to cellulose energy through mutualistic microorganisms that carry out fermentation in specialized digestive compartments.
story_beats.hint: cellulose fibers stopping at an animal-enzyme gate while mutualistic microbes open a fermentation route

story_beats.story: A cow taking a four-room stomach route while a horse is diverted to a separate enlarged-cecum hindgut route. The cow moves rumen → reticulum → omasum → abomasum while the horse bypasses that route and enters an enlarged-cecum/large-intestine fermentation path.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Ruminant stomach compartments.
story_beats.science: In a cow, a ruminant, the four stomach chambers are the rumen, reticulum, omasum, and abomasum. Mutualistic microorganisms digest cellulose in the rumen/reticulum; water is removed in the omasum; the abomasum carries out digestion with the cow's enzymes. Horses are not ruminants; they are hindgut fermenters that house cellulose-digesting microorganisms mainly in an enlarged cecum and large intestine.
story_beats.hint: a four-room cow route, with the horse diverted to a separate hindgut path

guided_journeys.tagline: A famous client’s protein has unfolded minutes before delivery. Rebuild it before the shipment leaves.
guided_journeys.premise: The Protein Factory is in emergency mode. A finished protein has lost its shape, and the client is waiting. Milo gives you the raw amino-acid pieces and tells you there is no shortcut: sequence, chemistry, folding, and assembly all have to work.
guided_journeys.mission: Rebuild the protein from amino acids, connect the chain correctly, follow the folding levels, and protect the finished structure from the denaturation furnace.
guided_journeys.finale: The rebuilt protein reaches the Function Showroom, folds correctly, and switches on its function lamp. Milo seals the package just before the loading door closes. The entire protein story now runs from sequence to structure to function.

scenes.story_open: Milo rolls in a damaged protein. The machine only works when a polypeptide reaches the right three-dimensional shape, and the rebuild starts with amino acids.
scenes.story_close: Milo places the damaged protein on a cart and sends you to the Amino-Acid Workbench to rebuild it from the smallest useful pieces.

story_beats.story: A folded-chain machine that powers a function lamp only after it takes a stable 3D shape. An unfolded chain passes through the folding gate; only the organized three-dimensional form switches on the function lamp.

story_beats.science: A protein consists of one or more polypeptide chains folded into a three-dimensional shape; protein shape determines function.
story_beats.hint: a folded polypeptide becomes a functional machine

story_beats.story: C, H, O, and N badges lock onto the common amino-acid frame while a sulfur badge appears only in a selected side-bin. C, H, O, and N badges stay on the common amino-acid framework; sulfur appears only on selected side chains and never receives an EVERY PROTEIN stamp.

story_beats.science: Protein amino acids necessarily contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen in their common backbone. Sulfur occurs in some amino acids, including cysteine and methionine, so sulfur is present in some proteins but is not an invariant element of every protein.

scenes.title: Amino-Acid Workbench
scenes.story_open: One amino-acid frame sits under a lamp: central carbon, hydrogen, amino group, carboxyl group, and one variable side chain.
scenes.story_close: The variable side chain on the amino-acid frame keeps changing, so Milo drops the pieces into the R-Group Sorting Tank.

story_beats.story: A central hub holding H, a carboxyl arm, an amine arm, and one changeable R backpack. The central carbon holds four attachments: hydrogen, carboxyl group, amine group, and the variable R group; the model stays conceptual rather than becoming an AP exact-structure drawing task.

scenes.title: R-Group Sorting Tank
scenes.story_open: Different R-group backpacks enter a water tank. Nonpolar ones avoid water; polar and charged ones behave differently, changing how the chain will fold.
scenes.story_close: Once the side-chain behaviors are sorted, the amino acids reach the Peptide-Tie Station and begin joining into a chain.

story_beats.story: One detachable backpack marked R that changes what happens when it is swapped. The same amino-acid frame receives different R backpacks, and each swap changes the side chain’s chemical behavior.

story_beats.science: Each amino acid has a variable side chain (R group) whose chemical properties differ among amino acids.
story_beats.hint: a detachable backpack marked R changes each amino acid's behavior

story_beats.story: An oily R backpack that turns away from surrounding water. The nonpolar backpack avoids the water-facing side of the tank and moves into the water-avoiding lane.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Nonpolar R group.
story_beats.science: R groups may be nonpolar/hydrophobic.

story_beats.story: An R backpack that reaches toward surrounding water droplets. The polar backpack turns toward the water-facing side of the tank and remains in the hydrophilic lane.

story_beats.science: R groups may be polar/hydrophilic.

story_beats.story: An R backpack carrying either a plus or minus magnet while remaining water-facing. A charged R backpack stays water-facing; the acidic lane carries a minus sign and the basic lane carries a plus sign at cellular pH.

scenes.story_close: The growing chain leaves the clamp and lands on the N/C Conveyor, which forces you to track its two different ends.

scenes.title: Four-Level Elevator
scenes.story_open: The elevator begins with primary structure and rises through increasingly complex levels. Every level contributes to the final functional form.
scenes.story_close: The elevator stops first at the Secondary Folding Room, where local backbone interactions create recognizable patterns.

story_beats.story: Floor 1 displaying only one linear ordered amino-acid chain. The elevator stops at Floor 1, where only the ordered amino-acid sequence is visible before any higher-level folding is shown.

scenes.title: Secondary Folding Room
scenes.story_open: Local regions of the chain fold into alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets through backbone hydrogen bonding.
scenes.story_close: Those local folds are only part of the job. The chain is pulled into the Tertiary Interaction Chamber for whole-chain folding.

story_beats.story: Local stretches of the backbone being pinned into coils and sheets by hydrogen bonds. Hydrogen-bond pins act on the polypeptide backbone and stabilize local coils and folds without yet representing the complete 3D fold of one chain.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Secondary structure.
story_beats.science: Secondary structure consists of local coils and folds of the polypeptide backbone produced by hydrogen bonding, including alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets.
story_beats.hint: Floor 2 folds local backbone segments into a helix or sheet

story_beats.story: A large α-shaped guide coiling one backbone segment into a spring while hydrogen-bond pins hold the coil. The α guide coils the local backbone segment and hydrogen-bond pins stabilize the resulting spring-like structure.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Alpha helix.
story_beats.science: Alpha helix is a secondary structure stabilized by hydrogen bonding within the polypeptide backbone.
story_beats.hint: a giant α/A winds into a spring-like helix

story_beats.story: A β marker laying neighboring backbone stretches across one pleated platform while hydrogen-bond pins connect them. Neighboring stretches of polypeptide backbone align across the pleated platform and are stabilized by hydrogen bonds; a SAME CHAIN POSSIBLE sign prevents the separate-chain misconception.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Beta-pleated sheet.
story_beats.science: A beta-pleated sheet is a secondary structure stabilized by hydrogen bonds between atoms of the polypeptide backbone in neighboring stretches of chain; separate polypeptide chains are not required.

scenes.title: Tertiary Interaction Chamber
scenes.story_open: The whole chain folds further as side chains interact through hydrophobic effects, hydrogen bonding, ionic interactions, and sometimes disulfide bridges.
scenes.story_close: When one folded chain is not enough, a loading door opens to the Quaternary Assembly Bay and multiple subunits arrive.

story_beats.story: One entire polypeptide folding into one overall three-dimensional shape inside a single-chain cradle. The cradle accepts exactly one polypeptide and folds the whole chain into its overall 3D shape through side-chain interactions.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Tertiary structure.
story_beats.science: Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of one polypeptide produced by side-chain interactions.
story_beats.hint: Floor 3 folds one polypeptide into its overall 3D shape

story_beats.story: Four required interaction stations plus one clearly optional close-contact station acting on side chains. The side-chain panel cycles through hydrogen-bond contacts, a hydrophobic huddle, plus/minus ionic attraction, and an S—S disulfide connection; a separate Campbell-only close-contact indicator represents van der Waals interactions.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Tertiary interactions.
story_beats.science: Tertiary protein structure is stabilized by side-chain interactions including hydrophobic interactions, van der Waals interactions, hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, and covalent disulfide bridges. story_beats.story: Two sulfur ends snapping together into one bright S—S bridge clamp. Two sulfur atoms from two cysteine side chains form one covalent S—S connection that helps stabilize tertiary structure.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Disulfide bridge.
story_beats.science: A disulfide bridge is a covalent bond formed between the sulfur atoms of two cysteine side chains and can help stabilize protein tertiary structure.
story_beats.hint: two sulfur atoms clasp into a bright S—S bridge

scenes.checkpoint_prompt: What exact scientific term matches this locked course definition? Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of one polypeptide produced by side-chain interactions.

scenes.title: Quaternary Assembly Bay
scenes.story_open: Multiple polypeptide subunits arrive at the assembly bay and combine into one functional protein when quaternary structure is required.
scenes.story_close: The assembled protein passes inspection, but Milo deliberately places an unfinished chain beside it at Raw Chain Inspection.

story_beats.story: Several folded subunits docking around a QUARTET sound-sign while a large MULTIPLE, NOT FOUR counter stays lit. Multiple folded polypeptide subunits dock into one protein assembly; the count display stays at “multiple” while the quartet sign serves only as the name cue.

scenes.title: Raw Chain Inspection
scenes.story_open: Milo stops the belt. A polypeptide chain is not automatically the same thing as a fully folded, functional protein.
scenes.story_close: To see why environment matters, the raw and folded chains are lowered into the Soluble-Protein Water Tank.

story_beats.story: A raw amino-acid chain on one side of an inspection gate and a folded working assembly on the other. The inspector labels the linear peptide-bonded chain as one category and only stamps the folded, organized one-or-more-chain assembly as the functional category.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Polypeptide versus protein.
story_beats.science: A polypeptide is a linear chain of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. A functional protein consists of one or more polypeptide chains folded and organized into a specific three-dimensional structure.
story_beats.hint: a raw amino-acid chain waits beside a folded working machine

scenes.title: Soluble-Protein Water Tank
scenes.story_open: A soluble protein enters water. Hydrophilic regions tend to face outward while hydrophobic regions are often buried away from the aqueous environment.
scenes.story_close: A temperature alarm suddenly sounds. The protein is rushed toward the Denaturation Furnace for the final stress test.

story_beats.story: Hydrophobic side chains moving inward while polar and charged side chains face the surrounding water. Inside the water tank, nonpolar/hydrophobic side chains tend to bury in the protein interior while polar and charged side chains tend to face outward; a membrane-protein warning prevents overgeneralization.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled R-group orientation in aqueous environments.
story_beats.science: For soluble proteins in an aqueous environment, nonpolar/hydrophobic side chains often become buried in the protein interior, while polar and charged side chains are often exposed to water. This pattern is context-dependent and should not be overgeneralized to membrane proteins.
story_beats.hint: hydrophobic side chains moving inward while polar and charged side chains face the surrounding water

scenes.title: Denaturation Furnace
scenes.story_open: The furnace temperature spikes. Higher-order interactions fail, the protein loses shape, and function can disappear even though peptide bonds are not being treated as ordinary heat-broken links.

story_beats.story: Heat or extreme conditions unfolding a working protein while an unbroken peptide-chain rail remains continuous. The stabilizing interactions are disrupted, the native 3D shape collapses, and function is lost while the peptide backbone remains intact under ordinary denaturing conditions.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Denaturation.
story_beats.science: Protein denaturation is loss of a protein's native three-dimensional structure, often causing loss of function, when conditions disrupt the interactions stabilizing the protein. In the packet's DNA context, 'denaturation' refers to separation of the two DNA strands when noncovalent base-pairing interactions are disrupted; it does not mean the phosphodiester backbone is hydrolyzed.

guided_journeys.learner_rule: Listen or read. Imagine the scene. Pause only at occasional Quick Recall cards. If recall is weak, ask for the scene or a hint; otherwise keep moving.
guided_journeys.narrative_design: One palace premise + one mission + one recurring guide + causal route + science-bearing actions + restrained distinctiveness. No decorative event may introduce a new scientific claim.

guided_journeys.tagline: A damaged archive has scattered the pieces of a genetic message.
guided_journeys.premise: A storm has damaged the Nucleic Acid Archive. Pages of a genetic manuscript have come apart into sugars, bases, phosphates, and paired strands. The archive will not reopen until the message is reconstructed in the correct direction.
guided_journeys.mission: Rebuild the manuscript from nucleotide parts, restore strand direction and pairing, and carry the recovered sequence safely through the melting room.
guided_journeys.finale: The repaired double helix locks into the archive case and the sequence catalog comes back online. Nia turns the key. You can now retrace how components become strands, how strands pair, and how sequence carries information.

scenes.story_close: The paired manuscript passes every base check, then enters the DNA Melting Room for one final test of strand stability.

scenes.title: DNA Melting Room
scenes.story_open: Heat begins separating the paired strands by disrupting noncovalent stabilizing interactions. GC-rich regions generally require higher temperatures under comparable conditions.

story_beats.story: An A–T pair displaying two dashed connections beside a G–C pair displaying three. The counters display two and three while a warning light blocks the inference that bond count alone determines melting behavior.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Base-pair hydrogen-bond count comparison.
story_beats.science: In DNA, an A–T base pair forms two hydrogen bonds and a G–C base pair forms three. The difference can contribute to stability, but hydrogen-bond count should not be encoded as the sole determinant of DNA duplex thermal stability.
story_beats.hint: A–T uses TWO dashed handshakes while G–C uses THREE

story_beats.story: Heat opening the paired DNA zipper while both sugar-phosphate rails remain continuous. Heat separates the complementary strands, but neither covalent sugar-phosphate backbone is cut.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is DNA denaturation.
story_beats.science: Heating can separate complementary DNA strands by disrupting the noncovalent interactions that stabilize the double helix; the covalent sugar-phosphate backbones remain intact in ordinary thermal denaturation.
story_beats.hint: heat opens the DNA zipper between the two strands without cutting either sugar-phosphate rail

story_beats.story: Two equal-length DNA sections heating side-by-side while the GC-richer section remains paired to a higher temperature and a context panel shows stacking, length, and ionic conditions. Under the same comparison conditions, the GC-richer section requires a higher temperature to separate, while the context panel prevents a hydrogen-bond-only explanation.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled GC content and thermal stability.
story_beats.science: DNA regions with higher G–C content generally melt at higher temperatures than equivalently sized lower-GC regions under comparable conditions. Do not explain this only by counting hydrogen bonds: DNA thermal stability also depends on nearest-neighbor sequence/stacking interactions, strand length, ionic conditions, and other thermodynamic factors.
story_beats.hint: two equal-length DNA sections heating side-by-side while the GC-richer section remains paired to a higher temperature and a context panel shows stacking, length, and ionic conditions

guided_journeys.tagline: A living-cell exhibit is losing its membrane as the temperature swings.
guided_journeys.premise: The Lipid Membrane Wing houses a living-cell exhibit. Tonight its membrane is failing: lipid pieces are scattered, fatty-acid tails are packing incorrectly, and the temperature control keeps swinging.
guided_journeys.mission: Rebuild the lipid components, assemble a phospholipid bilayer, identify the steroid framework, and use cholesterol to stabilize the membrane across temperature changes.
guided_journeys.finale: The final cholesterol molecules settle into the membrane and the thermostat stops oscillating. Lena watches the cell recover. The wing now tells one connected story about hydrophobic molecules, fat structure, bilayers, steroids, and membrane fluidity.

scenes.title: Lipid Lobby
scenes.story_open: Lena sweeps up oily molecules that avoid mixing with water. The wing contains several lipid types, and one of them will become the cell’s membrane.
scenes.story_close: One oily molecule rolls away from a water spill and lands beneath the Glycerol Hook Rack, where the first lipid components are waiting.

story_beats.story: An oil-rich molecular guest reaches the water fountain and beads away from it. The oil-rich guest avoids mixing with the fountain water, while a two-sided phospholipid marker shows that some lipids also contain a hydrophilic region.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Lipid.
story_beats.science: Lipids are a diverse group of molecules with substantial hydrophobic character because of their hydrocarbon-rich regions. Many are largely nonpolar, while phospholipids are amphipathic, with a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails. Lipids do not include true polymers.
story_beats.hint: an oil-rich molecular guest beads away from water

The directory sorts course examples into fats, phospholipids, and steroids; the cholesterol card remains within lipid examples and is later identified as a steroid.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Major lipid types.
story_beats.science: PPT emphasizes fats, phospholipids, and steroids; the CED also includes cholesterol within lipid examples.

scenes.title: Glycerol Hook Rack
scenes.story_open: A glycerol scaffold waits beside long fatty-acid tails. In a fat, three fatty acids join one glycerol.
scenes.story_close: Three fatty-acid tails swing from the rack and are carried to the Ester-Linkage Bench to be connected covalently.

story_beats.story: One central rack holds exactly three long fatty-acid tails. Three fatty-acid tails attach to one glycerol scaffold as a single fat assembly.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Fat composition.
story_beats.science: PPT describes fats as glycerol joined to three fatty acids.
story_beats.hint: one central rack holds exactly three long fatty-acid tails

story_beats.story: A GLITTER-ROLL spindle carries several alcohol-like OH hooks. The spindle presents hydroxyl-group hooks and then serves as the central scaffold to which fatty acids can attach in a fat.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Glycerol.
story_beats.science: PPT describes glycerol as an alcohol containing hydroxyl groups.
story_beats.hint: GLITTER-ROLL with hydroxyl hooks

story_beats.story: A long oily carbon-chain tail ends at one acidic carboxyl head. The long hydrocarbon region stretches across the tray while the carboxyl group stays fixed at one end, ready to join the glycerol scaffold.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Fatty acid.
story_beats.science: PPT describes fatty acids as long carbon chains with a carboxyl group at one end.

scenes.title: Ester-Linkage Bench
scenes.story_open: An ester-linkage clamp connects glycerol and fatty acids during dehydration.
scenes.story_close: The finished lipid model rolls onto the Fatty-Acid Tail Runway, where straight and kinked tails pack very differently.

story_beats.story: ESTHER closes a covalent clasp between the glycerol scaffold and a fatty-acid tail as a water droplet leaves. A dehydration event removes the equivalent of water while the covalent clasp forms between glycerol and a fatty acid.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Ester linkage.
story_beats.science: In a fat, fatty acids are covalently joined to glycerol by ester linkages formed through dehydration reactions. Exact lipid molecular structures are teacher-supporting material, not AP-required structural memorization.

scenes.title: Fatty-Acid Tail Runway
scenes.story_open: Straight saturated tails line one lane. Unsaturated tails carry C=C double bonds that create kinks, reduce tight packing, and increase room-temperature liquidity as unsaturation rises.
scenes.story_close: The runway ends at a storage door. The fat molecules disappear into the Fat Storage Vault, revealing why organisms keep them.

story_beats.story: A straight fatty-acid tail has only single carbon-carbon bonds and is filled with hydrogen markers. Because no carbon-carbon double bond interrupts the chain, the tail remains straight in the simplified course representation.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Saturated fatty acid.
story_beats.science: Saturated fatty acids contain only single bonds between carbon atoms; PPT describes them as having no C=C double bonds and more hydrogen.
story_beats.hint: straight hydrogen-full tail with no C=C

story_beats.story: A neighboring fatty-acid tail contains a C=C hinge and bends at the hinge. At least one carbon-carbon double bond interrupts the chain and produces the characteristic kink represented in the course scene.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Unsaturated fatty acid.
story_beats.science: Unsaturated fatty acids contain at least one C=C double bond.
story_beats.hint: C=C hinge creates a kinked tail

story_beats.story: One C=C hinge forces the tail to bend at that location. As soon as the C=C hinge locks in place, the previously straight runway tail bends.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Double-bond kink.
story_beats.science: A carbon-carbon double bond in an unsaturated fatty acid causes the carbon chain to kink.
story_beats.hint: one C=C hinge forces the tail to bend at that location

story_beats.story: A counter adds C=C hinges one by one and the unsaturation meter rises with each added hinge. Each added double-bond marker raises the unsaturation meter.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Unsaturation increases with double bonds.
story_beats.science: More double bonds in a fatty-acid tail mean greater unsaturation.
story_beats.hint: a counter adds C=C hinges one by one and the unsaturation meter rises with each added hinge

story_beats.story: Tails with more C=C hinges pack less tightly and the lipid sample flows more easily at room temperature. As double-bond hinges accumulate, tight packing is reduced in the representation and the room-temperature sample becomes more liquid.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Unsaturation and liquidity.
story_beats.science: Greater lipid unsaturation is associated with greater liquidity at room temperature.
story_beats.hint: tails with more C=C hinges pack less tightly and the lipid sample flows more easily at room temperature
