scenes.title: Fat Storage Vault
scenes.story_open: The vault is packed for long-term energy storage, while padded stations also represent cushioning and thermal insulation.
scenes.story_close: A membrane alarm interrupts the tour. Lena pulls out phospholipids and rushes you to the Phospholipid Pool Wall.

story_beats.story: A dense long-term energy vault sits beside a soft organ cushion and a subcutaneous insulating layer. Stored fat supplies a long-term energy reserve, adipose padding cushions organs, and subcutaneous fat reduces heat loss; a small cell-support marker retains the CED wording.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Fat functions.
story_beats.science: The major function of fats is long-term energy storage; adipose tissue also cushions organs and subcutaneous fat can provide thermal insulation. The current CED additionally frames fats as supporting cellular function.

scenes.title: Phospholipid Pool Wall
scenes.story_open: Phospholipids arrive with hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails. In water they self-organize into a bilayer with tails protected inside.
scenes.story_close: The bilayer stabilizes, but a rigid four-ring molecule is still unidentified. The next clue waits in the Steroid Ring Gallery.

story_beats.story: One glycerol scaffold holds two fatty-acid tails and a phosphate-containing head region. The head region remains on one side of the glycerol scaffold while exactly two fatty-acid tails extend from the other side.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Phospholipid.
story_beats.science: PPT describes a phospholipid as glycerol attached to two fatty acids and a phosphate-containing head region.
story_beats.hint: PHOSPHATE-headed membrane lipid with two tails

story_beats.story: The phospholipid head faces the surrounding water while its two oily tails turn away from the water. The head remains exposed to water and the tails orient away from water toward the protected interior.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails.
story_beats.science: PPT describes the phospholipid head as hydrophilic and fatty-acid tails as hydrophobic.
story_beats.hint: the phospholipid head faces the surrounding water while its two oily tails turn away from the water

story_beats.story: Many head-and-tail molecules arrange into two opposing rows with heads facing water on both sides and tails meeting in the middle. The molecules self-organize so hydrophilic heads face aqueous environments and hydrophobic tails cluster together in the interior, forming a double layer.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Phospholipid bilayer.
story_beats.science: Phospholipids assemble into bilayers in water and form lipid bilayers of plasma and cell membranes.
story_beats.hint: many head-and-tail molecules arrange into two opposing rows with heads facing water on both sides and tails meeting in the middle

scenes.title: Steroid Ring Gallery
scenes.story_open: Rigid four-ring frameworks fill the gallery. Testosterone is one steroid example, and some steroids function as hormones.
scenes.story_close: One steroid card is marked cholesterol and points toward the temperature controls at the Cholesterol Thermostat Gate.

story_beats.story: A rigid frame is built from four fused carbon rings, with interchangeable side-group tags clipped around the frame. The four rings stay fixed while the attached-group tags change from one steroid example to another.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Steroid.
story_beats.science: PPT identifies steroids by a four-fused-ring framework and states that attached groups distinguish steroid types.
story_beats.hint: four fused carbon-ring frame

story_beats.story: A TEST paper strikes a TONE bell mounted inside one four-ring steroid frame. The test paper hits the tone bell only inside a steroid frame, marking this molecule as one example rather than the definition of the whole steroid class.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Testosterone.
story_beats.science: PPT gives testosterone as an example of a steroid.
story_beats.hint: TEST paper strikes a TONE bell inside the steroid frame

story_beats.story: Only some four-ring frames enter a control panel with growth, development, metabolism, and homeostasis dials. Selected steroid molecules adjust the four process dials while other steroid frames, including the cholesterol display, remain outside the hormone-only lane.
story_beats.reveal: Keep the relationship labeled Steroid hormone functions.
story_beats.science: Steroids are lipids characterized by four fused carbon rings. Some steroids function as hormones that regulate processes such as growth, development, metabolism, and homeostasis; not every steroid is a hormone.

scenes.title: Cholesterol Thermostat Gate
scenes.story_open: Cholesterol wedges among phospholipids. At high temperature it restrains movement; at low temperature it interferes with tight packing, buffering membrane fluidity.

story_beats.story: A COAL-colored ESTHER ROLL wedges among animal-membrane phospholipids beside a thermostat. At higher temperature the wedge restrains phospholipid movement; at lower temperature it interferes with tight tail packing, buffering membrane properties across temperature changes.
story_beats.reveal: The exact name to attach to that image is Cholesterol.
story_beats.science: Cholesterol is a steroid and common component of animal cell membranes. It acts as a membrane-fluidity buffer, restraining phospholipid movement at higher temperatures and hindering tight packing at lower temperatures, thereby helping maintain membrane properties across temperature changes.
